item.text: {"text":"[NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) uses causal dilated convolutions and residual blocks to capture short- and long-range dependencies; its receptive-field expansion does not itself identify intent boundaries. Related 2024–2026 work supports adaptive intent modeling: [IMA/EMA](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10400839/) detects emerging intents and removes inactive ones during incremental adaptation; [CoDeR+](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) explicitly distinguishes demand shifts from incidental noisy clicks. Neither establishes a context-reset mechanism within NextItNet. The searched sources did not reveal a directly matching NextItNet reset method.\n\nResearch implication: test a jointly trained causal boundary gate inside one NextItNet network, attenuating convolutional contributions that cross inferred boundaries. This is a proposed extension, not a demonstrated result from these papers. Resetting only the final aggregation is insufficient if deeper residual states already contain older context; boundary control must cover convolutional paths and residual bypasses. Compare against static depth weights, input-dependent depth weights, and fixed recent-history truncation under matched training budgets. To demonstrate forgetting, replace or perturb the prefix before an inferred boundary while holding the suffix fixed, then measure changes in features and candidate scores. Gate values alone cannot establish effective forgetting. Evaluate whether repeated evidence of a shift produces stronger suppression than an isolated unusual interaction—the central ambiguity highlighted by CoDeR+."}
